# Beyond natural biology: rewiring cellular networks to study innate immunity

**Authors:** Lauren M. Landau; Jonathan C. Kagan

**Affiliations:** 1Division of Gastroenterology, Boston Children’s Hospital and Harvard Medical School, 300 Longwood Avenue, Boston, MA 02115, USA.

## Abstract

Within immune cells, microbial and self-ligands trigger pattern recognition receptors (PRRs) to nucleate and activate the signaling organelles of the immune system. Much work in this area has derived from observational biology of natural innate immune signaling. More recently, synthetic biology approaches have been used to rewire and study innate immune networks. By utilizing controllable chemical or optogenetic inputs, rearranging protein building blocks, or engineering signal recording circuits, synthetic biology-based techniques complement and inform studies of natural immune pathway operation. In this review, we describe recent synthetic biology-based approaches that have uncovered new insights into PRR signaling, virus-host interactions, and systemic cytokine responses.

## Introduction

In the infancy of immunological research over a century ago, many discoveries were derived purely from observation. To understand phagocytosis, a scientist simply peered into a microscope and watched as phagocytes surrounded and attempted to devour a splinter in the transparent body of a starfish larva [1]. Decades passed before immunologists developed genetic and other manipulations to glean further insights into the diverse molecular pathways of the immune system. Network level observations are now possible, with genome- or proteome-wide analysis of gene expression and regulation emerging as common techniques in immune system biology. The large amounts of data generated by such ‘omics approaches have revealed examples of context-specific molecular activities, which raises questions concerning the underlying network design principles (Figure 1). Studies of innate immune pattern recognition receptors (PRRs) have benefitted from such network analyses. As much of the molecular analysis of innate immunity has been performed in the post-genomic era, experimental studies of individual PRRs led to the bioinformatic identification of protein families. Representative PRR families include the Toll-like Receptors (TLRs), RIG-I like Receptors (RLRs), and Nucleotide binding domain leucine-rich repeat containing (NLR) proteins. Each protein in these families binds distinct microbial or self-derived molecules to induce overlapping and distinct inflammatory responses. Detailed investigation into the biochemical activities governing TLR, RLR, and NLR pathways has revealed shared and divergent molecular interactions controlling each response. Several recent reviews have covered this topic, which will not be discussed in detail here [2–4].

The most common contemporary approaches to study PRR activities are conceptually akin to those used over 100 years ago – observations of natural cellular behavior. However, conceptually distinct strategies to study immune system functions have recently emerged, whereby natural biology is replaced with redesigned cellular networks. By exploiting the modular information processing of cells, scientists can reengineer cellular functions and pressure-test biological causality to uncover novel aspects of natural pathway operation. This strategy of cellular redesign is commonly referred to as synthetic biology [5]. Synthetic biology can be defined as any engineered biological functionality that has not been evolved by nature. Early breakthroughs in cell engineering, such as the use of restriction enzymes, ectopic overexpression of transgenes, or GFP tags, have already had an impact on the research community. As time progresses, these manipulations are becoming increasingly creative, and this review aims to highlight how recent synthetic biology-based approaches have revealed novel aspects of innate immune signaling.

### Dissecting innate immunity through synthetically engineered PRR pathways

PRR signal transduction networks are designed such that diverse receptors feed into shared downstream effectors using conserved biochemical mechanisms. For example, upon microbial detection, most PRRs seed the assembly of large cytosolic protein complexes known as supramolecular organizing centers (SMOCs), which represent the signaling organelles of our innate immune system [6]. Examples of SMOCs include the myddosome (seeded by TLRs), the MAVS complex (seeded by RLRs), the inflammasome (seeded by NLRs), and the STING oligomer (assembled by enzymatic products of the PRR cGAS). Despite the biochemical diversity of their components, each SMOC contains one or more receptors, adaptors, and effector proteins. These proteins respectively contain domains responsible for ligand binding, scaffolding, and enzymatic activity. The flexibility of the building blocks within SMOCs provides an opportunity to recombine pieces of natural proteins to build new functional interactions (Figure 2). To explore this potential for signaling modularity, the interferon (IFN)-inducing effector domain from the protein STING, known as a pLxIS motif [7], was appended on MyD88 and caspase-1, which are core components of myddosomes and inflammasomes. Expressing MyD88-pLxIS and caspase-1-pLxIS chimeric proteins in macrophages endowed the myddosome and inflammasome with IFN activity [8]. Based on this finding, synthetic SMOCs composed of pLxIS motifs fused to multimers of the oligomerizing protein FKBP were engineered to stimulate IFN responses in macrophages [8].

Similar approaches have been taken to explore the protein NLRP1, which is a key regulator of inflammasomes in humans. Ribotoxic stress was thought to activate inflammasome activities, with a disordered region (DR) within NLRP1 being implicated in this stress response [9]. To explore the sufficiency of the DR for stress responses, a hybrid protein was engineered by fusing this region of NLRP1 to the enzymatic domains of the related inflammasome component CARD8. The ability of this chimeric protein to induce inflammasome activities in keratinocytes in response to ribotoxic stress revealed the sufficiency of the NLRP1 DR to sense the ribotoxic stress response [9]. These approaches therefore showcase the sufficiency of protein motifs as modular signaling units in the innate immune system.

Another use of synthetic biology has been to explore the importance of protein subcellular positions for PRR activities. One example involved replacing the localization domain in the adaptor TIRAP, which signals downstream of TLRs at the plasma membrane and endosomes. To determine the relative importance of each subcellular position of TIRAP, the natural localization domain was replaced with phosphoinositide-binding domains that were specific for lipids present at the plasma membrane or endosomes. Macrophages expressing these chimeric proteins revealed subsets of TLRs that were capable of signaling from either subcellular position. This finding explained the importance of TIRAP localization through its promiscuous phosphoinositide-binding domain, as this property enabled the activation of differentially localized TLRs [10]. In a similar manner, studies of synthetic STING proteins revealed organelle-specific innate immune activities. STING normally resides in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) but traffics through the conventional secretory pathways towards lysosomes upon innate immune activation [11]. Fusion of STING with the transmembrane domains of the endosomal protein transmembrane protein 192 (TMEM192) promoted STING accumulation in the endolysosomal compartment. This approach revealed the predisposition for post-Golgi STING activation [12]. Improved organelle-targeting capabilities have also been applied to engineering mitochondria-specific transcriptional activator-like effector nucleases (TALENs) that cause cleavage and degradation of mitochondrial DNA. This tool has been applied to illustrate how mitochondrial DNA double-strand breaks (mtDSBs) cause mitochondrial herniation and release mitochondrial RNA into the cytoplasm to activate RIG-I-mediated IFN-I responses [13].

Protein chimeras are additionally critical tools for identifying innate immune protein functions in understudied species. The widespread sequencing of genomes over the last two decades has revealed hundreds of PRRs whose functions and mechanisms of action are unknown. Mechanistic observational biology is limited in many species, as genetic tools are largely unavailable for most organisms. As such, synthetic biology has served as a surrogate approach to define activities of candidate PRRs found in non-model organisms. For instance, fusion of the TLR ectodomain from the chordate Branchiostoma lanceolatum to the intracellular Toll/interleukin-1 receptor (TIR) domain of human TLR2 induces NF-κB activation in response to double-stranded RNA, suggesting an antiviral function for BlTLR [14]. Using protein chimeras to redesign immune signaling pathways can even reveal the existence of similar pathways elsewhere in nature. For example, the human PRR caspase-4 is unable to cleave IL-1β upon binding bacterial lipopolysaccharides (LPS) [15]. Using residues from other caspases, caspase-4 was redesigned to sense LPS and cleave IL-1β as well as the pore-forming protein gasdermin-D. The signaling capacity of this synthetic system led to the discovery of multiple natural carnivoran species that encode a caspase-4 with this activity [16]. With limited tools available to study non-model organisms in situ, synthetic biology approaches leverage advanced mammalian tools to learn about other species.

### Optogenetic tools to study innate immunity

One of the most powerful types of engineered interactions involves light-inducible proteins, which allow for cellular manipulations with spatiotemporal resolution. At the forefront of this field is the light-dependent oligomerizing protein cryptochrome 2 (CRY2), derived from Arabidopsis thaliana. This protein undergoes rapid and reversible homo-oligomerization in response to blue light [17]. Just as synthetic chemically-inducible SMOCs can be engineered, CRY2-based light-inducible assembly of the myddosome has facilitated mechanistic studies of innate immune activation. Optogenetic control of this SMOC has revealed endosomal TLR-independent activation of IRF7 downstream of myddosome assembly [18]. Optogenetic-controlled polymerization of such complexes typically relies on nucleation barriers that enable the immune system to respond decisively to small numbers of stimuli. This principle governs the CARD-BCL10-MALT1 (CBM) complex that signals downstream of the PRR Dectin-1 to activate the inflammatory transcription factor NF-κB [19]. By fusing CARD9 to CRY2 to nucleate the CBM complex independently of upstream factors, it was elucidated how the supersaturation of BCL10 in resting cells promotes CBM signaling independently of its polymer structure [20]. Similarly, CRY2 was fused to caspases and other death effectors to generate rapid and efficient light-inducible pyroptosis, apoptosis, and necroptosis. This system was used to study the fate of different forms of cell death at a single cell level, revealing differential cytoskeletal rearrangements in neighboring cells and preferential extrusion of pyroptotic and necroptotic cells from epithelia [21]. Alternative optogenetic systems rely on analogous plant-based phototropins such as the LOV2 domain from Avena sativa, which forms the basis for the light-inducible nuclear localization signal (LINuS) system [22]. By using this platform to inducibly control protein transport, viral proteomes were probed for nuclear transport inhibition, leading to the identification of matrix proteins from Isfahan virus and Jurona vesiculovirus that can suppress host nuclear transport [23].

Light-operated systems have the unique ability to achieve non-invasive, traceless, and precise spatiotemporal manipulations at the organismal level. For example, far-red light-controlled immunomodulatory engineered cells (FLICs) release IFN-β, tumor necrosis factor alpha (TNF-α), and IL-12 upon illumination, providing a tool to examine the effects of cytokine release at particular sites in vivo. Implantation of FLICs in a mouse melanoma model promoted an increase in Natural Killer cells and antigen-specific CD8+ T cells that contributed to anti-tumor immunity and central memory T cell responses [24]. Additionally, the introduction of a photoactivable adenylyl cyclase (AC) from Beggiatoa sp. into macrophages enabled the study of AC-dependent macrophage regulation. This platform uncovered the effects of AC signaling to suppress pro-inflammatory cytokine signaling and regulate cardiac inflammation in situ [25]. [25]. Overall, optogenetic approaches have enhanced our ability to investigate innate immune signaling with versatility and precision.

### Engineering outputs for cellular monitoring

Rewiring the molecular networks in cells can be used to manipulate cellular outputs to report on specific immune signaling activities. Certain approaches exploit natural processing steps and engineer them to generate measurable outputs. For example, C-tag TNF is an encoded reporter of TNF maturation that takes advantage of natural proteolytic cleavage of the pro-inflammatory cytokine [26]. By engineering detectable exposure of a cryptic epitope upon pro-TNF cleavage, this system enables the study and visualization of TNF release at single-cell resolution. Thus, it was applied in a genetic screen to identify regulators of TNF maturation, such as the vesicle trafficking factor AP2M1 [27]. Another technique incorporated fluorescent protein binding sites in viral genomes to endow infected cells with the ability to report on their interactions. This CRISPR-assisted single viral genome tracking (CASVIT) technology integrates the dCas9 binding sequence CRISPR-Tag into the HSV-1 genome, enabling multicolor spatially resolved real-time tracking of viral replication and host-virus interactions. This tool revealed interactions between multiple replication compartments within a cell, as well as the loss of telomeric and centromeric DNA due to viral replication [28].

Living cells have further been engineered with functionalized memory to track immune responses over time. Implementation of signal recording circuits has been instrumental in monitoring inaccessible locations in real time. For example, the use of NF-κB- or IRF5-inducible CRISPR RNAs (crRNAs) triggers parallel dCas12a-mediated targeted mutations in the endogenous AAVS1 safe harbor locus. This permanently records a cell’s history of inflammation with temporal resolution and multi-signal tracking [29]. Because bacteria naturally reside in the gastrointestinal tract, they can also serve as useful tools for monitoring immune activities at the organismal level [30]. Commensal E. coli strains have been engineered to contain synthetic memory devices that can detect and respond to the reactive oxygen species (ROS) product tetrathionate for 6 months in the mouse gut. This platform enables non-invasive long-term monitoring of subclinical levels of inflammation, and has revealed dynamic tetrathionate production during S. typhimurium infection and inflammatory bowel disease models [31]. Thus, the development of genetically encoded reporters and memory circuits has enabled precise and real-time monitoring of signaling dynamics and cellular responses to immune stimuli.

### Future Perspectives

To date, we have witnessed a new wave of immunological engineering in the rising era of synthetic biology and expect this trend to grow stronger in the coming decades. While synthetic systems face certain restrictions in applicability and artificiality, synthetic biology offers new tools and strategies to accelerate the development, enhance the performance, and address the current limitations of innate immune research practices. While the progress in applying these tools for basic research has been the focus of this review, they can and are being leveraged for therapeutic uses as well [32]. The development and use of inventive synthetic biology tools and out-of-the-box-thinking can enable scientists to make pioneering discoveries and push science in new directions [33].

Examples of new experimental directions that are possible derive from several new synthetic biology developments in other fields. For example, chromosome-free bacterial SimCells could be used to dissect the contribution of DNA to PRR sensing in phagocytes [34], light-triggered trafficking of secretory synaptic proteins using the zapERtrap platform could be designed to study immunological cytokine secretion [35], CRISPR-based epigenetic editing can enable the study of immune cell lineage identity and persistent gene expression [36], or light-induced split-Cre recombinase systems can achieve spatiotemporally-targeted genome engineering in vivo [37]. By borrowing techniques and approaches from other areas of synthetic biology, researchers can expand the tools available to modulate and study innate immune responses.
